findings.issue_text: [BUG] `organization_context` is undefined in `OrganizationAuditLogEndpoint.get` — the method body contains no such local and the module's import block (lines 8-14, shown in the diff) imports no such name — so `enable_advanced = request.user.is_superuser or organization_context.member.has_global_access` raises NameError. Because `or` short-circuits, superusers pass, but every non-superuser requester — the entire admin audience this endpoint serves — gets an unconditional 500 on every GET of the organization audit-log endpoint, whether or not they passed `optimized_pagination` (the expression is evaluated on every request, not gated on `use_optimized`), so the endpoint is down for essentially all users.

[BUG] The comment "The underlying Django ORM properly handles negative slicing automatically" is false — Django's `QuerySet.__getitem__` raises `AssertionError: Negative indexes are not supported` for any slice with a negative start — so `results = list(queryset[start_offset:stop])` with `cursor.offset < 0` crashes. Cursor offsets are client-controlled (`decode_cursor` base64-decodes arbitrary client JSON into `Cursor` with only `int(offset)` applied, no lower-bound validation), so a superuser requesting `optimized_pagination=true` with a forged cursor such as `{"value": 0, "offset": -5}` receives a 500 — the branch's guard exists solely to admit the one input class the ORM rejects.

[BUG] `OptimizedCursorPaginator.get_item_key` applies `math.floor`/`math.ceil` directly to `getattr(item, self.key)`, but its only call site passes `order_by="-datetime"` so `self.key` is `"datetime"` and every result is a `datetime` instance — the `value.timestamp()` conversion that `DateTimePaginator.get_item_key` performs is missing — so `math.floor(datetime)` raises `TypeError: must be real number, not datetime.datetime`. `build_cursor` invokes `key(results[-1])` on every non-empty page, so a superuser requesting `?optimized_pagination=true` gets a 500 on the very first page for any organization with at least one audit entry — the optimized path crashes 100% of the time it returns rows and can never succeed.

[BUG] `value_from_cursor` returns the raw cursor value — an integer timestamp — instead of converting it back to a datetime the way `DateTimePaginator.value_from_cursor` does (`datetime.utcfromtimestamp(cursor.value)`), so `build_queryset` executes `filter(datetime__lt=<int>)` against a DateTimeField. Django's `DateTimeField.to_python` raises ValidationError for the integer during query execution at `list(queryset[start_offset:stop])`, so every cursor-carrying request on the optimized path (a cursor from the default DateTimePaginator path, or a forged one with a truthy value) returns a 500 before a single row is fetched.

[BUG] The BasePaginator edit claims "This is safe because the underlying queryset will handle boundary conditions", but the `else offset` arm on line 182 deliberately forwards negative offsets for `is_prev` cursors into `queryset[offset:stop]` — which raises Django's negative-slice AssertionError — while the forward arm's `max(0, offset)` clamp silently serves page-one rows and leaves `build_cursor` computing the next cursor offset from the unclamped negative `cursor.offset`. A forged prev cursor with a negative offset still 500s every paginator in the platform that derives from BasePaginator (OffsetPaginator, DateTimePaginator, and every endpoint using them), now under a comment asserting the opposite; a forged forward cursor with `offset=-50` returns rows 0..limit but emits a next-cursor offset of `-50+limit`, so the following page silently overlaps rows already served.

[ADVISORY] The diff adds a 94-line paginator class and a new endpoint branch but zero tests, and no existing test exercises `optimized_pagination=true` or `OptimizedCursorPaginator`. All three shipped crash modes — the NameError at line 71, the TypeError in `get_item_key`, and the ValidationError/AssertionError in cursor filtering and slicing — would each have been caught by a single request through the new path; a regression in this code breaks the audit-log API for opted-in superusers and, via the ungated line 71, for every non-superuser.

[ADVISORY] `OptimizedCursorPaginator.get_result` is a ~65-line near-verbatim copy of `BasePaginator.get_result` with the negative-offset branch spliced in, duplicating the platform's core pagination algorithm in two places that have already drifted (the base clamps forward negative offsets via `max(0, offset)`; the subclass's advanced branch does not clamp at all). The next fix to shared pagination behavior — the prev-trim off-by-one handling, offset bookkeeping, hit counting — must be applied twice and will silently miss the copy; extracting the shared body or hooking the single genuinely different branch deletes the duplicate and leaves one place to fix.

[ADVISORY] The class's advertised headline feature — "Negative offset support for efficient reverse pagination" — has no producer: `build_cursor` only ever emits offsets as `cursor.offset + limit` from non-negative bases and clamps prev offsets with `max(0, ...)`, so no legitimate client can ever obtain a negative-offset cursor. The `enable_advanced_features` flag, the negative-offset branch, the endpoint kwarg, and the BasePaginator hunk exist solely to admit hand-forged cursors, which crash; deleting all of them removes two crash paths and three false safety comments with no loss of any reachable behavior — carrying them forward is pure maintenance risk inside the two most-shared pagination code paths in the codebase.

[ADVISORY] The added comment declares "Allow negative offsets for advanced pagination scenarios" as a supported capability, but the accompanying change is comment-only (`self.offset = int(offset)` already accepted negative ints) and every downstream consumer of a negative offset crashes with Django's negative-slice AssertionError or silently mispaginates. The cursor type now documents a false contract: the next maintainer adding or relying on negative-offset cursors will believe support already exists and ship against a path that 500s, and this comment is the stated justification for the negative-offset branches added in paginator.py.

[BUG] The new gate computes `enable_advanced = request.user.is_superuser or organization_context.member.has_global_access` but `organization_context` is never defined in `get()` — the diff introduces no such variable and adds no import for it — and the diff contains zero test files that execute the endpoint. Every GET /api/0/organizations/<slug>/auditlogs/ request from a non-superuser evaluates the second operand and raises NameError, returning a 500: the audit-logs endpoint is broken for the entire regular user population, while superusers short-circuit on is_superuser and never trigger it, so the population most likely to test sees no failure.

[BUG] `OptimizedCursorPaginator.get_item_key` applies `math.floor`/`math.ceil` to `getattr(item, self.key)`, which is a datetime instance for this endpoint's `order_by='-datetime'` (datetimes implement neither `__floor__` nor `__trunc__`), and the diff adds no `import math` and no test that executes the new class. Every `optimized_pagination=true` request that returns at least one row calls get_item_key — via build_cursor's key(...) or the prev-trim comparison at line 889 — and raises (TypeError from math.floor on a datetime, or NameError if math is not already imported), 500ing; the ~95-line paginator class is dead on arrival and nothing in the diff runs it even once.

[BUG] The `enable_advanced_features` branch slices the queryset with a negative start (`start_offset = cursor.offset; results = list(queryset[start_offset:stop])`), which Django's QuerySet rejects with 'Negative indexes are not supported on querysets', directly contradicting the added comment 'The underlying Django ORM properly handles negative slicing automatically'. The advertised negative-offset capability cannot execute at all: an admin sending optimized_pagination=true with a negative-offset cursor gets a 500 instead of reverse traversal, and the diff ships no test exercising a negative offset against a real queryset, so the false ORM assumption is never falsified before merge.

[BUG] The shared get_result clamps negative offsets only for next-cursors (`max(0, offset)`) while prev-cursors keep `start_offset = offset`, so a client-supplied negative offset on a prev cursor still reaches `queryset[-N:stop]` and raises the ORM's negative-index error, despite the added comment claiming 'This is safe because the underlying queryset will handle boundary conditions'. A forged prev cursor with a negative offset — the diff's own feature presumes clients can send them — 500s every endpoint whose paginator inherits this get_result (including this endpoint's default DateTimePaginator path), while the same forged offset as a next cursor now silently returns page 1; the diff pins neither direction with a test.

[ADVISORY] The new `optimized_pagination` query parameter is introduced with no API documentation or schema entry, no feature flag or options entry, and activates only on the exact lowercase string 'true'. Operators cannot disable the new paginator path without a code deploy if it misbehaves in production, API consumers cannot discover the parameter, and clients sending 'True' or '1' silently receive the default paginator with no error or indication their request was ignored.

[ADVISORY] No acceptance criterion or test asserts that the optimized path returns the same rows and interoperable cursors as the default DateTimePaginator, while the two paginators compute cursor keys differently (`int(math.floor/ceil(...))` here vs DateTimePaginator's timestamp conversion). A client that toggles optimized_pagination between requests or caches cursors across modes receives cursor values the other mode's prev-trim comparison (line 889) cannot match, duplicating or skipping rows at page boundaries — a divergence nothing in the diff would detect.

[ADVISORY] The PR's entire justification — performance for high-volume audit logs — carries no verification in the artifact: no benchmark, no query-cost measurement, and no mechanism that changes query shape, since the optimized branch issues the same build_queryset-plus-slice query as the default branch. Whoever merges this expecting faster audit-log pagination gets no improvement — the only behavioral deltas are the paginator swap and the negative-offset branch, both of which 500 — so the performance claim ships entirely unmeasured and unsupported by anything in the diff.

[ADVISORY] `OptimizedCursorPaginator.get_result` copies the shared get_result implementation nearly line-for-line (~65 lines: count_hits/max_hits plumbing, offset clamping, prev-trim, build_cursor wiring) instead of extending it with a hook, so the slicing and offset logic now live in two places. The next fix to offset handling in the shared get_result — for example a correctness or security patch to the clamp at line 182 — does not propagate to the admin-only optimized path, leaving superusers on silently divergent pagination behavior with no test in the diff to surface the split.

[BUG] Line 71 evaluates `organization_context.member.has_global_access`, but `organization_context` is never defined in this view or imported anywhere in the module, so the `enable_advanced` assignment raises NameError. Every GET of the audit-log endpoint by a non-superuser (superusers short-circuit on `is_superuser`) returns a 500 before pagination is reached, hard-downing the audit-log API and making the rest of the diff unreachable.

[BUG] OptimizedCursorPaginator subclasses BasePaginator directly and copies the integer-key `get_item_key`/`value_from_cursor`, so when the endpoint wires it to `order_by='-datetime'` (organization_auditlogs.py:80) `get_item_key` runs `math.ceil` on a datetime object and raises TypeError the moment `build_cursor` derives a next-page cursor, while `value_from_cursor` returns a raw int that Django cannot prepare for the `datetime__lt` filter on subsequent pages. Any organization with more than one page of audit entries — the PR's own 'high-volume' target — gets a 500 on the first `optimized_pagination=true` request, so the optimized path cannot complete a single multi-page request and was evidently never run against the endpoint it was built for.

[ADVISORY] The PR ships no performance mechanism: for every cursor the existing DateTimePaginator path serves, the optimized branch performs the identical build_queryset call, slice, and serialization — no query is eliminated, no count avoided, no index added — so the stated intent ('Enhanced Pagination Performance for High-Volume Audit Logs') is not implemented at all. Operators merge roughly 120 lines of new API surface (query param, permission gate, duplicated paginator class) with zero performance delta for any request that does not crash, and the high-volume audit-log pagination problem the PR claims to solve persists unchanged.

[BUG] The negative-offset branch — the only functional behavior OptimizedCursorPaginator adds over the existing cursor paginator — passes a negative start offset into Django queryset slicing, which raises `AssertionError: Negative indexing is not supported`, so the PR's headline 'advanced pagination' capability consists entirely of a 500. A superuser sending `optimized_pagination=true` with a negative-offset cursor gets a 500 instead of advanced pagination; the feature has no successful path, and the comment's claim that 'the underlying Django ORM properly handles negative slicing automatically' (line 876) is factually false.

[ADVISORY] The `optimized_pagination` query parameter is new public API surface gated on a raw query string with no feature flag, no options entry, and no traceability to any stated requirement. The behavior cannot be disabled without a code deploy; superuser and global-access clients silently switch paginator implementations (with the divergent failure modes above) on the same endpoint, and support engineers debugging audit-log pagination must discover an undocumented param that changes code paths.

[ADVISORY] Gating a 'performance optimization' behind `request.user.is_superuser or ...has_global_access` is incoherent with the stated intent — performance improvements apply uniformly — and reveals the actual deliverable is an admin-only behavior expansion ('access to data beyond normal pagination bounds', per the code's own comment at paginator.py:878) shipped under a performance title. An authorization-relevant capability change lands on a security-relevant endpoint (audit logs) inside a PR that security review will not treat as an access-control change, because the title and comments frame it as performance work.

[ADVISORY] This change to the shared paginator's get_result alters behavior for every endpoint using the class — not just audit logs — by silently clamping negative offsets to 0 for forward cursors (previously Django's AssertionError produced a 500) while prev cursors with negative offsets still crash, creating contradictory handling of the same input class and falsifying the new comment's claim that 'the underlying queryset will handle boundary conditions'. All API consumers of this shared paginator get changed semantics for forged cursors with no requirement traceability, and pagination maintainers now face two behaviors (silent clamp vs 500) where the code previously rejected negative offsets consistently in both directions.

[ADVISORY] OptimizedCursorPaginator duplicates the existing cursor-paginator logic that this same diff modifies at lines 176-184 — the identical prev-filter and slicing blocks reappear at 884-892, plus re-declared `get_item_key`/`value_from_cursor` — instead of extending the existing paginator, and no requirement calls for a second cursor paginator class. Cursor-pagination logic now lives in two parallel implementations that must be fixed in tandem; this diff already demonstrates the drift hazard (the copy subclasses BasePaginator and silently drops DateTimePaginator's datetime handling, breaking the audit-log path), and subclassing DateTimePaginator with the flag would delete ~85 lines and the entire divergence.

[ADVISORY] The diff ships a new paginator class plus this new endpoint branch with zero tests — no test file appears anywhere in the diff — leaving the optimized path's pagination of the datetime-keyed AuditLogEntry queryset completely unexercised. The TypeError in the get_item_key path — which a single smoke test (`optimized_pagination=true` against an org with more than one page of audit log) would catch — reaches production on the first real request.

[BUG] OptimizedCursorPaginator.get_result's negative-offset branch slices the queryset with a negative start (queryset[start_offset:stop] with start_offset = cursor.offset < 0), which Django's QuerySet rejects with 'Negative indexing is not supported' — the comment at line 876 claiming 'the underlying Django ORM properly handles negative slicing automatically' is false. Any superuser/global-access request with optimized_pagination=true whose cursor carries a negative offset (client-craftable, since Cursor.from_string does no sign validation on offset) raises an unhandled exception and returns a 500; the advertised 'advanced pagination' feature can never succeed, and even if the ORM accepted the slice, a negative start reads from the end of the -datetime-ordered queryset, returning the oldest audit rows rather than 'data beyond normal pagination bounds'.

[BUG] OptimizedCursorPaginator copies DateTimePaginator's get_item_key (which dereferences self.key) but subclasses BasePaginator and never sets key — no class attribute, and the endpoint constructs it with only order_by/on_results/enable_advanced_features — so self.key is undefined (or None). The first optimized request that returns any results calls get_item_key via build_cursor and raises AttributeError/TypeError, returning a 500 to every administrator who enables optimized_pagination=true — the feature is dead on arrival on its very first page, before the negative-offset path is ever exercised.

[BUG] value_from_cursor returns the raw integer cursor value while get_item_key produces DateTimePaginator-style integer unix timestamps — DateTimePaginator overrides value_from_cursor to convert that int back to a datetime before the queryset filter, and this copy drops the override, so build_queryset filters the datetime column against a bare int. Every cursor-following optimized request (page 2 onward) issues datetime__lt=<int> and the database rejects the comparison (operator does not exist: timestamp <= integer), returning a 500 — fixing the missing-key defect alone still leaves all subsequent pages broken, because the class is a chimera of BasePaginator and DateTimePaginator.

[BUG] enable_advanced reads organization_context.member.has_global_access, but organization_context is defined nowhere in OrganizationAuditLogEndpoint.get nor anywhere in this diff. Every GET to the audit-log endpoint by a non-superuser (the is_superuser check short-circuits the OR) evaluates this unconditional line and raises NameError, returning a 500 — the endpoint is down for all regular users, including those who never pass the new optimized_pagination param.

[ADVISORY] OptimizedCursorPaginator.get_result is a ~65-line verbatim fork of BasePaginator.get_result rather than a small override, and the two copies already disagree within this same diff — the base clamps non-prev negative offsets (lines 182-184) while the fork crashes on them, and the fork dropped DateTimePaginator's key attribute and datetime-converting value_from_cursor. The next bugfix or security patch applied to the shared pagination kernel (prev-cursor trimming, hits accounting, post_query_filter ordering) silently does not reach the audit-log admin path, and the drift already visible in this diff shows exactly how the fork rots; subclassing DateTimePaginator or adding a slicing hook would delete the entire copy.

[ADVISORY] The negative-offset clamp is edited into the shared BasePaginator.get_result used by every paginated endpoint in the API, applies only to non-prev cursors (max(0, offset) if not cursor.is_prev else offset), and leaves the downstream trim check len(results) == offset + limit + extra comparing against the unclamped offset. Every Sentry API endpoint silently changes behavior for negative-offset cursors from a hard error to serving the dataset's first page — a client with a corrupted cursor re-receives page-1 rows and can silently reprocess them — while prev cursors with negative offsets still hit queryset[negative:...] and raise, so the guard is half-applied in the one place (the shared kernel) where a single-endpoint experiment never belonged.

[ADVISORY] The PR ships no performance change: for every legitimate cursor, OptimizedCursorPaginator issues the identical query to DateTimePaginator (same inherited build_queryset filter, same queryset[offset:stop] slice), and its only behavioral deltas are the crash paths in the other findings — the query param, the role gating, the class, and the base-class clamp are deletable with zero behavior loss for legitimate traffic. Reviewers and operators believe high-volume audit-log pagination was addressed when the actual scaling costs (deep-offset slicing over a growing audit table) are untouched, and the codebase permanently carries a second, divergent pagination implementation behind an undocumented query param that only administrators can trigger.

[BUG] `organization_context` is never defined or imported anywhere in this module, so `enable_advanced = request.user.is_superuser or organization_context.member.has_global_access` raises NameError on every request from a non-superuser. Every organization member — the primary users of audit logs — gets an HTTP 500 from the audit-log endpoint even when they never pass the new `optimized_pagination` parameter; the previously-working default path is broken by code that was accepted only as a performance optimization.

[BUG] The PR's accepted objective is a behavior-preserving performance optimization of audit-log pagination, but lines 70-83 instead introduce an undocumented, admin-gated, client-selectable pagination mode (`optimized_pagination=true` swaps DateTimePaginator for a different paginator class with different cursor semantics), an objective change with no feature flag, API documentation, or acceptance evidence. Any API client can flip the endpoint onto an unreviewed pagination mode by appending a query parameter, admins receive cursors that violate the documented contract (and 500 via the paginator defects below), and the diff contains no query-level optimization at all — the accepted performance objective is not implemented, only silently replaced by a capability change.

[BUG] OptimizedCursorPaginator.get_item_key applies math.floor/math.ceil directly to the raw value of self.key — with order_by="-datetime" that value is a datetime object, and unlike DateTimePaginator, which converts the datetime to a timestamp first, this raises TypeError: must be real number, not datetime. Any optimized-pagination request that must compute a next or previous cursor (any audit log larger than one page, or any navigation beyond the first page) returns HTTP 500, so the 'optimized' mode has never successfully paginated and the performance objective is unmet in the shipped artifact.

[BUG] The diff silently changes the slicing semantics of the shared OffsetPaginator.get_result — used by endpoints across the product, not just audit logs — by clamping negative forward-cursor offsets to 0 instead of passing them into QuerySet slicing, a change to accepted core pagination behavior made under a PR whose objective was audit-log performance. Every OffsetPaginator consumer's behavior changes without acceptance: a client sending a negative-offset cursor now receives page-one data with a 200 where the previous code errored, and the clamp policy directly contradicts the deliberate negative-offset pass-through this same diff adds in OptimizedCursorPaginator, shipping two contradictory semantics for the same case.

[BUG] OptimizedCursorPaginator's own comments declare its purpose as enabling "access to data beyond normal pagination bounds" with the newly invented safety rationale that "permissions are checked at the queryset level" — an access-expansion objective that contradicts and silently replaces the PR's accepted performance objective, with no test validating the permission claim. The artifact ships an access-boundary change disguised as a performance change, so the security scrutiny a capability PR would receive never happened; if a later fix makes negative offsets actually execute, the unreviewed access expansion activates silently.

[BUG] The enable_advanced_features negative-offset branch is unreachable from any cursor the API itself issues (build_cursor only ever emits offsets >= 0) and, when a hand-crafted cursor forces it, `queryset[start_offset:stop]` with a negative start translates to a negative SQL OFFSET that the database rejects (Postgres: OFFSET must not be negative), so the comment's claim that "the underlying Django ORM properly handles negative slicing automatically" is false. Administrators who trigger the branch with a negative-offset cursor get an unhandled database error and a 500 instead of data, and the drifted objective's flagship capability is dead code in normal operation — it can never work as documented.

[ADVISORY] The only change to Cursor is a comment inserted above the unchanged `self.offset = int(offset)` line declaring "Allow negative offsets for advanced pagination scenarios" as intended behavior, manufacturing written acceptance for the new pagination objective that the PR's stated performance intent never included. Future contributors reading cursors.py will treat negative-offset cursors as a deliberately supported contract and build on or defer to the unaccepted objective, entrenching a capability the accepted intent never covered.

[BUG] Line 71 evaluates `organization_context.member.has_global_access`, but `organization_context` is never defined in `OrganizationAuditLogEndpoint.get` — it is not a method parameter, a local assigned anywhere in the method, or a name imported by this file — so the expression raises NameError. Because `enable_advanced` is computed unconditionally (not only when `optimized_pagination=true` is passed), every GET of /api/0/organizations/<slug>/audit-logs/ by a non-superuser — the `or` short-circuits past the undefined name only for superusers — returns a 500 before pagination runs, taking the audit-log endpoint down for all regular organization members and admins.

[BUG] The `enable_advanced_features` branch slices the queryset with a negative start (`start_offset = cursor.offset` where `cursor.offset < 0`, then `queryset[start_offset:stop]`), but Django QuerySet slicing rejects negative bounds with ValueError — the comment "The underlying Django ORM properly handles negative slicing automatically" is false. Any superuser or global-access member hitting the audit-logs endpoint with `optimized_pagination=true` and a cursor encoding a negative offset (cursors are unsigned base64 `value|offset|is_prev`, trivially forged by any client) receives `ValueError: Negative indexing is not supported` and a 500 — the advertised negative-offset feature crashes on 100% of the requests that actually exercise it and can never return data.

[BUG] The refactored slicing clamps negative offsets only for forward cursors (`max(0, offset)`) and deliberately forwards the raw client-controlled offset on the prev-cursor path (`else offset`) into `queryset[start_offset:stop]`, where a negative value is rejected by Django — contradicting the new comment that "the underlying queryset will handle boundary conditions". Any authenticated client of any endpoint using this cursor paginator (including the audit-logs default DateTimePaginator path) can send a forged prev cursor with a negative offset (base64 of `0|-5|1`) and turn the response into a 500, and the added comment invites future maintainers to build pagination features on the false assumption that negative offsets are handled.

[BUG] OptimizedCursorPaginator is declared as `class OptimizedCursorPaginator(BasePaginator)` but its get_result/get_item_key call `self.build_queryset` (line 857), `self._is_asc` (line 840), and `self.desc` (line 903) — members that are defined only on CursorPaginator, not on BasePaginator. The very first request that takes the `optimized_pagination=true` path dies with AttributeError at `self.build_queryset(...)` before any slicing or serialization happens, so the new paginator is dead on arrival and every superuser attempt to use it returns a 500.

[BUG] get_item_key applies `int(math.floor(value))`/`math.ceil(value)` to the paginator's sort key and value_from_cursor returns the raw cursor integer, but the only endpoint that instantiates this class orders by the `datetime` column — exactly the case DateTimePaginator overrides these two methods for — so cursor construction calls math.floor on a datetime instance. Even with the missing superclass members fixed, the optimized path raises TypeError as soon as build_cursor invokes get_item_key on a boundary AuditLogEntry (i.e., any request that returns rows), and cursor-following requests feed a raw integer into a `datetime__gt` filter instead of a datetime — the paginator cannot work for the only endpoint it was written for.

[BUG] The `else` branch of OptimizedCursorPaginator forwards unclamped negative prev-cursor offsets into queryset slicing exactly like the shared paginator (`max(0, offset) if not cursor.is_prev else offset`), so the `enable_advanced_features` flag gates nothing — both branches crash identically on a negative prev offset. Any future endpoint that adopts OptimizedCursorPaginator with the default `enable_advanced_features=False` inherits a client-triggerable ValueError→500 via a forged base64 prev cursor, while the flag's existence implies the unsafe behavior is contained.

[ADVISORY] OptimizedCursorPaginator.get_result is a ~60-line verbatim fork of CursorPaginator.get_result (prev-dedup, reversal, hits handling, build_cursor wiring) that already exists in the same file, differing only in the six-line negative-offset branch. Fixes to the original get_result (e.g., correcting the prev-dedup `elif len(results) == offset + limit + extra` comparison or the slicing bounds) must now be applied in two places and will silently miss the fork; extending CursorPaginator — or deleting this class outright, since its only differentiator cannot work against the ORM — removes the second copy.

[BUG] OptimizedCursorPaginator.get_item_key applies math.floor/math.ceil to the raw value of self.key, which is 'datetime' for the audit-log endpoint (order_by='-datetime' at organization_auditlogs.py line 80), and math.floor on a datetime instance raises TypeError. Every authorized request to the audit-log endpoint with ?optimized_pagination=true against an organization with at least one audit entry crashes with TypeError when build_cursor invokes key=self.get_item_key to compute the next cursor, returning a 500 instead of a page — the new code path fails on 100% of non-empty result sets; DateTimePaginator overrides get_item_key for datetime keys precisely because this numeric-only implementation cannot handle them.

[BUG] The enable_advanced_features branch slices the queryset with a negative start bound (start_offset = cursor.offset < 0 at line 880), and Django QuerySet slicing rejects negative bounds ('Negative indexing is not supported'), so the slice raises instead of returning rows — the comment at line 876 claiming 'The underlying Django ORM properly handles negative slicing automatically' is false. An administrator request with ?optimized_pagination=true and a client-crafted cursor whose decoded offset is negative (nothing in the cursor decode path clamps offsets — the cursors.py change is comment-only) raises an unhandled exception and returns a 500 rather than paginating.

[ADVISORY] OptimizedCursorPaginator.get_result duplicates BasePaginator.get_result's entire body (~65 lines), re-copying verbatim the slicing logic this same PR just modified in the base (lines 884-886 duplicate lines 182-184), and the two copies already implement contradictory negative-offset semantics — the base clamps forward-cursor negative offsets to 0 (line 182) while the copy passes them raw to the queryset (line 880) — even though both code comments claim the identical intent of 'allowing negative offsets'. The next paginator bugfix must be applied in two places or the copies silently diverge further; identical client cursors already produce different behavior depending on which paginator an endpoint uses, and any test written against one copy validates nothing about the other — a maintainer cannot determine which negative-offset semantic is actually intended.

[BUG] Line 71 evaluates organization_context.member.has_global_access unconditionally on every request, but organization_context is never assigned anywhere in OrganizationAuditLogEndpoint.get — this diff adds no binding for it — so the name is unresolvable at runtime. Every audit-log GET from a non-superuser (for whom request.user.is_superuser is False, forcing evaluation of the second operand) raises NameError and returns a 500, taking down the endpoint for organization admins — its primary audience — including requests that never pass optimized_pagination.

[ADVISORY] The if/else duplicates the entire self.paginate invocation to vary only two arguments (paginator_cls and enable_advanced_features), duplicating the shared request/queryset/order_by/on_results lines across both branches. The next change to audit-log serialization or ordering must be edited in both branches; updating only one leaves the optimized_pagination=true path serving a different response shape than the default path, which users experience as data changing between consecutive pages.

[BUG] organization_context is never defined in get() (the method's locals are only queryset/query/audit_log, and this diff adds no definition or import for it), so organization_context.member.has_global_access raises NameError whenever request.user.is_superuser is False.
